chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from his father, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who travels to his farm over a period of two or three days, and his route passes by the farms of his paternal uncles' sons; does he shorten the prayer and break the fast, or does he complete [the prayer] and fast? He said, 'He does not shorten [the prayer] and he does not break the fast.'

key_terms.بَرِيدَيْنِ: Two days (or two stages of travel)
key_terms.يُقَصِّرُ: Shortens the prayer (performing two rak'ahs instead of four)

ai.seo_question: Does a traveler shorten their prayer and break their fast if the journey lasts two or three days?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the scholar clarifies that a traveler on a journey of two to three days does not shorten their prayers (qasr) nor break their fast, effectively treating the journey as a period of full ritual observance. This ruling highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding the definition of 'travel' (safar) and the conditions under which concessions are granted, emphasizing that duration alone does not automatically trigger the traveler's exemptions if the person maintains their routine. The hadith underscores the principle that legal rulings are often contingent upon specific circumstances and the traveler's intent, rather than rigid temporal markers.
